Calibration curves showed agreement between predicted and observed survival. Decision-curve analysis suggested potential clinical utility within the evaluated thresholds. In a separate exploratory comparison in the external primary-tumor subset (n = 82), C-indices were 0.746 for RDCS and 0.590 for the official Sarculator application. CONCLUSION: RDCS estimates OS after complete RPLS resection using preoperative CT-derived imaging signatures and postoperative clinicopathologic information. RDCS may complement established postoperative prognostic tools, but its application in surveillance and clinical management requires prospective validation and clinical impact assessment.

articles.title: Axial spondyloarthropathy with peripheral joint involvement mimicking gout on ultrasound: A case of double contour sign pitfall.
articles.abstract: Axial spondyloarthropathy (axSpA) may present with peripheral joint involvement, which makes the diagnosis more challenging when axial symptoms are unrecognized. In this report, a 66-year-old man presented with chronic left knee pain and swelling as the initially recognized musculoskeletal manifestation of axSpA. A double contour sign (DCS)-like appearance near the fibular head and a DCS at the first metatarsophalangeal joint initially suggested gout. Subsequent evaluations, including dual-energy CT, sacroiliac joint CT and MRI, and HLA-B27 testing, led to a diagnosis of axSpA with peripheral joint involvement. This case highlights diagnostic pitfalls in musculoskeletal ultrasound, particularly the gout-specific DCS. It also emphasizes the importance of correlating imaging findings with clinical symptoms and pain distribution.

articles.title: Externally validated MRI radiomics machine learning models for differentiating between myxoid liposarcoma and myxoma.
articles.abstract: OBJECTIVE: To develop and externally validate a radiomics-based machine learning model for differentiating myxoid liposarcoma (MLS) from myxoma on MRI and compare its diagnostic performance with that of experienced musculoskeletal radiologists. METHODS: In this retrospective study, T1-weighted and fluid-sensitive MRI sequences from 109 patients with histologically confirmed MLS or myxoma were used to train support vector machine (SVM), random forest (RF), and XGBoost (XGB) classifiers. Models were evaluated in an independent external cohort of 32 patients from a second institution using different scanner hardware and protocols. Diagnostic performance was compared with that of two fellowship-trained senior musculoskeletal radiologists. Secondary analysis assessed MLS grading. RESULTS: The T1-weighted SVM achieved the strongest external binary performance (accuracy, 0.84; AUC, 0.91), outperforming RF and XGB (p = 0.005 and p < 0.001, respectively). Its performance did not differ significantly from that of radiologists (AUC, 0.88-0.94; p > 0.05), although the study was not powered to establish equivalence. Fluid-sensitive SVM performance was limited (accuracy, 0.56; AUC, 0.60), indicating sequence-dependent generalizability. Models and radiologists demonstrated limited MLS grading accuracy, reflecting tumor heterogeneity. CONCLUSION: Externally validated radiomics-based machine learning supported noninvasive differentiation of MLS from myxoma primarily on T1-weighted MRI. T1-weighted SVM performance was not significantly different from that of experienced radiologists, although equivalence was not established, whereas fluid-sensitive performance was substantially weaker. T1-weighted quantitative imaging biomarkers may complement soft tissue tumor characterization, but extrapolation to fluid-sensitive sequences requires caution.

articles.title: Metaphyseal changes on whole-body magnetic resonance imaging following bisphosphonate therapy in children with chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis: distinguishing treatment effect from disease flare.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic nonbacterial osteomyelitis (CNO) is an autoinflammatory disease that often affects the metaphyses. Bisphosphonates, a second-line therapy, can cause bone marrow changes that may mimic active disease. OBJECTIVE: To characterize metaphyseal long-bone marrow changes on whole-body MRI (WB-MRI) following bisphosphonate therapy in children with CNO and evaluate if they can be distinguished from active disease. MATERIALS AND METHODS: Retrospective study (2015-2025) included children with CNO treated with bisphosphonates and age- and sex-matched untreated controls. Two blinded pediatric radiologists independently evaluated long-bone metaphyses for CNO and bisphosphonate treatment effects classified as symmetric sclerotic bands, alternating high-signal and sclerotic bands, or predominantly high-signal bands. Associations with treatment, number of infusions, and intervals from the first to most recent infusions were evaluated, accounting for repeated examinations. RESULTS: Twenty-one treated children (median age 10.7 years, 12 females) underwent 30 pretreatment and 51 post-treatment WB-MRIs; 21 controls (median age 10.0 years, 12 female) underwent 48 examinations. Bisphosphonate-related changes occurred in 85.7% (18/21) treated children versus 14.3% (3/21) controls (P<0.001). Sclerotic bands alone occurred in 23.8% versus 14.3%. Alternating high-signal-intensity and sclerotic bands (38.1%) and predominantly bright signal bands (23.8%) occurred exclusively after treatment. High signal was associated with more infusions (P<0.001) from the most recent (P<0.001) and first (P=0.027) infusions and was most common around the knee and distal tibia. CONCLUSION: Symmetric metaphyseal high-signal stripes are a dose- and time-related bisphosphonate treatment effect and should not be misinterpreted as active CNO. Sclerotic bands alone are not specific for treatment.

articles.title: Explainable vision transformer framework for breast lesion classification with Grad-CAM support.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Given that breast cancer remains the most lethal malignancy among women globally, there is an urgent need for reliable and comprehensible diagnostic technology. Deep learning models have demonstrated encouraging outcomes in breast imaging; nevertheless, existing methodologies struggle to encompass global context and deliver clinically relevant justifications for their conclusions. METHOD: The ExViT-Breast framework was trained and internally validated on CBIS-DDSM (n = 1,566 subjects; masses and calcifications), externally validated on INbreast, and evaluated across modalities on the BUSI ultrasound dataset. A Vision Transformer backbone with a cross-view attention fusion module integrated paired craniocaudal (CC) and mediolateral oblique (MLO) mammographic views. Four explainability methods were compared: Grad-CAM, Grad-CAM++, LayerCAM, and Transformer-LRP. Classification performance was assessed by AUC and sensitivity at one false positive per examination. Explanation quality was evaluated using faithfulness (deletion/insertion curves), clinical plausibility (pointing game against expert-defined lesion regions), and ensemble-based uncertainty estimation. Model calibration was quantified using Expected Calibration Error (ECE). RESULTS: ExViT-Breast achieved superior diagnostic performance with an AUC of 0.94 ± 0.02 on CBIS-DDSM, significantly outperforming conventional CNN architectures (ResNet-50: AUC = 0.89, p < 0.001) and single-view Vision Transformers (AUC = 0.91, p = 0.003). External validation on INbreast demonstrated robust generalization (AUC = 0.91 ± 0.03), while cross-modality evaluation on BUSI yielded AUC = 0.88 ± 0.04. Transformer-LRP consistently provided the highest explanation quality across all datasets, achieving faithfulness scores of 0.71 ± 0.05 and plausibility rates of 79.5% on CBIS-DDSM, significantly superior to Grad-CAM variants (p < 0.001). CONCLUSION: The ExViT-Breast framework demonstrates the potential of explainable Vision Transformers in breast imaging, combining high classification performance with clinically interpretable explanations. The integration of multi-view analysis and quantitative explainability assessment positions this approach as a promising tool for computer-aided diagnosis in breast cancer screening and detection. CLINICAL TRIAL: Clinical trial number: not applicable.

articles.title: Adaptive Liver Stiffness Quantification in Magnetic Resonance Elastography Using a Heterogeneity-Aware Deep Learning Framework.
articles.abstract: Magnetic resonance elastography (MRE) enables non-invasive liver stiffness measurement (LSM). However, accurate quantification remains operator-dependent particularly for identifying clinically valid measurement regions and selecting a representative sampling strategy. This study developed and validated a fully automated, heterogeneity-aware deep learning framework that integrates valid-region identification, elastogram heterogeneity assessment, and a study-specific adaptive quantification strategy, while substantially reducing analysis time. The framework was evaluated in a prospective cohort of 201 subjects. Magnitude images and wave-attenuation images were combined to identify valid regions for LSM. Because spatial stiffness heterogeneity may increase sensitivity to region-of-interest (ROI) placement, elastograms were classified as homogeneous or heterogeneous using a multimodal convolutional neural network-deep neural network (CNN-DNN) classifier that integrates spatial image features with quantitative stiffness descriptors. For homogeneous elastograms, a study-specific distributed circular-ROI reduced-sampling strategy was evaluated, whereas volumetric sampling was applied to heterogeneous elastograms to better capture spatial variations in stiffness. The segmentation module achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.894 ± 0.035, an Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.810 ± 0.057, and a 95th-percentile Hausdorff-Distance (HD95) of 5.45 ± 4.05 mm. Automated LSMs showed excellent agreement with expert measurements (ICC = 0.998; Bland-Altman bias = 0.007 kPa), while reducing analysis time from approximately 15 min to 0.35 s/patient. The heterogeneity classifier achieved accuracies of 89.4% and 88.5% at the slice and patient-levels, with areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUCs) of 0.928 and 0.935, respectively, demonstrating substantial patient-level agreement with the expert reference classification (Cohen's κ = 0.770). By integrating automated valid-region identification with objective elastogram heterogeneity assessment, the framework may improve standardization and reproducibility of LSM.

articles.title: Blank-Image Ablations Can Mislead: A Mismatched-Image Control for Visual-Requirement Audits in Medical-VQA-Evidence from ERA-TurkMed, A Turkish Generative System.
articles.abstract: Whether a Medical Visual Question Answering (Medical-VQA) system uses its image is usually tested by replacing it with a zero tensor: if performance does not drop, the image is deemed unused. We show that this test can mislead. We built ERA-TurkMed, to our knowledge the first generative Medical-VQA system for Turkish radiology (frozen BiomedCLIP, Q-Former, LoRA-adapted Llama-3.1-8B), trained by a three-stage curriculum on a single-center, ethics-approved dataset (~ 5000 chest radiographs; ~ 17,476 question-answer pairs). On the full test set (n = 3454, three seeds), BLEU-4 is higher without the image (Δ =  - 0.024 ± 0.007, seed-level p = 0.025). A mismatched-image control-an in-distribution radiograph of a different patient-reverses this conclusion: the real image is better on polarity accuracy (+ 0.035, p = 0.030), chrF (+ 0.018, p = 0.020), and exact match (+ 0.015, p = 0.028) in all three seeds. The blank-image advantage is confined to the BLEU family and the hallucination rate, and reverses on polarity accuracy, a measure validated against manual annotation (95.0% agreement) that exposes the negation blindness of clinical-term F1. The visual contribution is nonetheless small: 77.2% of test questions recur verbatim in training, and an image-free retrieval baseline matches the model on clinical-term F1 (0.496 vs. 0.510), a consequence of template-based, AI-assisted dataset construction rather than of Turkish. We therefore recommend verbatim-overlap auditing, an image-free baseline, a mismatched-image control, and negation-sensitive metrics as standard. Code is available; model weights follow upon publication. The clinical data cannot be shared under Turkish data-protection law (KVKK).

articles.title: Deep Learning Radiomics to Predict Vessels Encapsulating Tumor Clusters and Prognosis in Hepatocellular Carcinoma Based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-Enhanced MRI.
articles.abstract: Vessels encapsulating tumor clusters (VETC) are significantly associated with poor prognosis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), with implications for patient survival and clinical management. This study aimed to evaluate a deep learning (DL) radiomics model based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI for preoperative prediction of the VETC pattern in HCC. Patients with pathologically confirmed HCC who underwent Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI between January 2016 and August 2024 were retrospectively enrolled. Visually assessed radiological features were collected to construct a clinical-radiological (CR) model. Deep learning and handcrafted radiomics features were extracted from arterial, portal venous, and hepatobiliary phases. Feature selection and DL radiomics model construction were performed using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO). Multivariable logistic regression was applied to develop a hybrid model and corresponding nomogram. Model discrimination was quantified using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Cox regression analysis was performed to identify predictors of recurrence-free survival (RFS). In the training cohort, the hybrid DL-radiomics nomogram yielded the highest AUC (0.92), compared with 0.87 for the DL model, 0.80 for the radiomics model, and 0.74 for the CR model. However, standalone DL model showed better discriminative performance in the internal validation cohort, with an AUC of 0.87, sensitivity of 0.80, and specificity of 0.87. VETC status, AST level, and intratumoral necrosis were identified as independent predictors of RFS and incorporated into the VAI prognostic model. The VAI model achieved an AUC of 0.75 (95% CI, 0.68-0.80), which was significantly higher than those of three conventional prognostic systems (range, 0.52 [95% CI, 0.46-0.59] to 0.58 [95% CI, 0.51-0.64]). The hybrid DL-radiomics model based on Gd-EOB-DTPA-enhanced MRI showed favorable discriminative performance for VETC prediction in the training cohort, while the standalone DL model demonstrated better performance in the internal validation cohort. The VAI model enables individualized prediction of postoperative RFS for patients undergoing hepatectomy.

articles.title: Auditing Report Order in Emergency Teleradiology Using Routine Event Logs.
articles.abstract: This study aims to describe recorded report-order inversions in emergency teleradiology and assess their interpretation when assignment and active interpretation times are unavailable. We reconstructed computed tomography (CT) transmissions from July 2025 through June 2026, requiring a unique exact linkage and stable priorities. An inversion occurred when a later examination received its first recorded report before an earlier examination still unresolved at the same provider. Eligible head-abdomen pairs were analyzed using dependence-preserving intervals, an empirical conditional reference and secondary models incorporating retrieved imaging workload proxies. Among 8170 examinations, 6,051 had the standard ED urgent category. Later head CT inverted 1060/1761 earlier-abdomen pairs (60.2%; 95% confidence interval, 57.5-62.7%); later abdominal CT inverted 154/1038 earlier-head pairs (14.8%; 12.3-17.5%). Observed-minus-reference differences were - 4.5 percentage points (- 7.3 to - 1.6) and - 11.4 (- 14.2 to - 8.8). Counts were usable for 3474/3565 target examinations and 2665 pairs. Report-order asymmetry did not demonstrate preferential dispatch. Observed inversion proportions were below the empirical conditional reference probabilities. This does not establish protective scheduling. Routine exports support a descriptive audit; additional workflow events are necessary to identify mechanisms or compare dispatch policies.

articles.title: Predicting Findings from Radiology Indication Text: BERT vs Naïve Bayes Classification.
articles.abstract: This retrospective study evaluated Naïve Bayes (NB) and transformer-based BERT models for predicting findings from radiology order Indication text for use in radiology informatics and automated worklist triage systems. From the MIMIC-CXR-JPG dataset, 219,995 chest radiograph orders were extracted, and the indication text was paired with CheXpert-generated labels for a binary (findings/none) and multi-label (13-category) classification task. Three BERT models (baseBERT, radBERT, BioClinicalBERT) were compared to NB classifiers using bootstrap confidence intervals, McNemar's test, and paired permutation tests. Precision-recall curves assessed triage utility under a high-precision constraint. On the binary task, all BERT models significantly outperformed NB on AUROC (0.793-0.798 vs. 0.763; P < 0.001  ). The radBERT model did better on AUROC than baseBERT and BioClinicalBERT (0.798 vs. 0.793 for both; P < 0.001  , DeLong test) by a small but statistically significant amount. On the multi-label task, NB had better micro-F1 at the default threshold (0.399 vs. 0.361-0.388; P < 0.001  ), but the BERT models had better AUPRC (0.470-0.475 vs. 0.358) and calibration (expected calibration error 0.011-0.016 vs. 0.077). NB's apparent advantage was due to its overconfident probabilities, not overall superiority. At a 90% precision constraint, radBERT recalled 55.0% of positive orders (36,557 examinations triaged per 100,000 annual orders). At 95% precision, radBERT maintained an actionable recall of 26.4%, whereas NB's recall collapsed to near zero. The modest edge of radBERT over general-domain and clinical-note-pretrained variants on the binary task suggests the distinctive character of Indication text limits the benefit of domain-specific pretraining. Order Indication text contains actionable information for predicting imaging findings, supporting transformer-based models for automated radiography triage systems.

articles.title: Postdeployment Performance of a Commercial Artificial Intelligence System for Pulmonary Nodule Detection at Chest CT: Examination-Level Agreement, Clinical Indication, and Image-Based Review Across 13,536 Examinations.
articles.abstract: Postdeployment performance of pulmonary nodule detection AI is rarely measured. This retrospective, cross-sectional analysis of prospectively collected routine data evaluated a commercial detection system (ClearRead CT; Riverain Technologies), deployed with a candidate-size threshold of greater than 3 mm, across 13,536 consecutive chest CT examinations at one academic center (January 2025-January 2026). Final reports, classified by natural language processing (NLP; validated against manual review of 896 reports: sensitivity 99.5%, specificity 99.6%, κ 0.99), served as the examination-level comparator; randomly selected discordant examinations were reviewed on images. Because radiologists viewed AI output before reporting, report-referenced results are presented as agreement; accuracy estimates are given only after image review. AI was positive in 9142 examinations (67.5%) and reports documented a nodule in 3919 (29.0%). Positive percent agreement was 80.6% (95% CI 79.4, 81.8), negative percent agreement 37.8%, and report-referenced positive predictive value 34.6%; 5982 examinations (44.2%) were AI positive/report negative, and Cohen κ was 0.13 (maximum attainable, 0.33). Agreement was 98.6% for screening, 38.3% for oncologic, and 32.6% for inpatient/emergency examinations, which contributed 76.1% of discordance. On image review, 291 of 298 (97.7%) AI-positive/report-negative examinations contained only non-nodule structures, and 196 of 198 (99.0%) AI-negative/report-positive examinations contained an unmarked nodule larger than 3 mm, 45 of them (23.0%) larger than 6 mm. Review-adjusted examination-level sensitivity was 81.2%, specificity 38.2%, and positive predictive value 35.4%. These findings describe one configuration at one institution; performance should be measured locally, by indication, and against image review.

articles.title: The Impact of High Intensity Focused Ultrasound on Ovarian Reserve in Women with Uterine Fibroids and Adenomyosis: A Systematic Review and Single Arm Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: The aim of the study is to evaluate the effect of high-intensity focused ultrasound (HIFU) treatment on ovarian reserve by synthesizing available evidence on post-treatment changes in ovarian reserve markers. Studies were eligible if they evaluated the impact of HIFU on ovarian reserve by reporting pre- and post-treatment ovarian reserve markers, including anti-Müllerian hormone (AMH), antral follicle count (AFC), or gonadotropin levels. MEDLINE, Scopus, and CENTRAL were searched from inception to January 5, 2026. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts, assessed full texts, and evaluated risk of bias using the Cochrane Risk-of-Bias tool for randomized trials or the JBI critical appraisal tool for case series. Disagreements were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer. Of 2498 records identified, 1935 were screened after removal of duplicates, 24 articles underwent full-text review, and 10 studies were included in the systematic review and single-arm meta-analysis. This review included 2 randomized controlled trials and 8 case series (n = 667). The duration of follow-up after HIFU ranged between 3 and 24 months. Overall pooled analysis of all studies showed a small but statistically significant reduction in serum AMH levels (MD = -0.12 ng/mL; 95% CI = -0.20 to -0.04, I2 = 0%). Pooled analysis of AFC (2 studies, n = 140) revealed no statistically significant change after HIFU treatment (MD = -0.05; 95% CI = -0.28 to 0.19; I2 = 0%). The reduction in AMH persisted when the analysis was restricted to fibroid-only studies (MD = -0.13 ng/mL; 95% CI = -0.22 to -0.05), whereas data were insufficient for an adenomyosis-specific estimate. Pooled single-arm analysis showed a small but statistically significant reduction in serum AMH levels following HIFU treatment, with no significant change in AFC. This decline was associated with, rather than proven to be caused by, HIFU treatment, as the available evidence derives predominantly from uncontrolled pre-post studies that cannot establish causality. Therefore, evaluation of ovarian reserve after HIFU should not rely on AMH alone but incorporate AFC and clinical context. Pre-treatment counseling is particularly important in women with diminished ovarian reserve or of late reproductive age, in whom even minor reductions may be clinically relevant.

articles.title: Microvascular and Macrovascular Complications and Their Associated Risk Factors Among Patients with Type 2 Diabetes in Saudi Arabia: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a major public health challenge in Saudi Arabia and is associated with substantial morbidity through vascular complications. This systematic review and meta-analysis estimated the pooled prevalence of diabetes-related complications and examined study-level risk factors among Saudi adults with T2DM. Methods: The review followed PRISMA guidance and was registered in PROSPERO (registration number: CRD420251032235). Random-effects models were used, and heterogeneity, risk of bias, small-study effects, subgroup effects, influence, and study-level moderators were assessed. Results: Of 743 records identified, 36 unique, non-overlapping datasets contributed to at least one quantitative synthesis. Study quality was good in 25 studies (69.4%). Pooled prevalences were 24% for retinopathy (95% CI 18-30%; 26 studies), 16% for nephropathy (11-23%; 22 studies), 24% for neuropathy (16-34%; 27 studies), 3% for cerebrovascular stroke (2-6%; 10 studies), 10% for myocardial infarction (MI) and broader coronary heart disease/coronary artery disease (CHD/CAD) (6-15%; 16 studies), 5% for peripheral arterial disease (PAD; 2-11%; 10 studies), and 10% for diabetic foot (4-26%; nine studies). Heterogeneity was extreme (I2 = 93.5-99.3%), and prediction intervals were wide. Excluding influential outliers left pooled estimates essentially similar but reduced τ2. In meta-regression, no moderator was significantly associated with retinopathy, stroke, or diabetic foot prevalence (all p > 0.05). For nephropathy, longer diabetes duration (β = -0.254, 95% CI -0.411 to -0.097, p = 0.005; 52.5% of between-study variance) and female proportion (β = 0.036, 95% CI 0.005 to 0.067, p = 0.026; 18.8%) were significant. For neuropathy, smoking prevalence was significant (β = 0.093, 95% CI 0.001 to 0.185, p = 0.047; 18.8%). For PAD, female proportion was inversely associated with prevalence (β = -0.084, 95% CI -0.147 to -0.021, p = 0.015; 53.2%). Region explained 84.5% of the heterogeneity in MI/CHD/CAD, with lower estimates in Tabuk and Taif, and HbA1c explained 24.5% of the heterogeneity in stroke (p = 0.167). Year of publication explained <10.0% of the heterogeneity in every parsimonious model. Substantial residual heterogeneity remained in all models (residual I2 83.0-99.9%). Individual studies also frequently reported associations of complications with poor glycemic control, longer diabetes duration, hypertension, dyslipidemia, obesity, smoking, and physical inactivity. Conclusions: Diabetes-related complications impose a substantial burden in Saudi adults with T2DM, but estimates vary markedly across populations, clinical settings, and diagnostic definitions. The findings support standardized screening and improved primary research using consistent case definitions; study-level meta-regression findings should be interpreted cautiously.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence in Acute Coronary Syndromes: From Early Diagnosis to Culprit Lesion Characterization, Coronary Physiology, and Risk Stratification.
articles.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is being investigated across the acute coronary syndrome (ACS) care pathway, including early diagnosis, coronary lesion characterization, procedural guidance, and risk prediction. This comprehensive review examines the current evidence across the entire ACS trajectory, with particular emphasis on clinically actionable and interventional applications. AI-enabled electrocardiography (ECG) may improve detection of myocardial infarction, including occlusion myocardial infarction (OMI) that does not meet conventional STEMI criteria. Models combining clinical data and high-sensitivity troponin may improve early rule-out and rule-in. In coronary imaging, AI can quantify plaque characteristics and assist with the interpretation of OCT and IVUS, while image-derived physiology may help assess non-culprit lesions. However, better diagnostic accuracy does not necessarily translate into better revascularization decisions. AI-based models can also estimate post-ACS ischemic, bleeding, and mortality risk, although evidence that their use improves treatment or outcomes remains limited. The next priority is prospective evaluation of whether these tools improve decisions, workflow, and patient outcomes across diverse clinical settings.

articles.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence Models in Breast Cancer Diagnosis: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background: This systematic review aims to evaluate and synthesize the current research on generative artificial intelligence (AI) models, focusing on their roles, performance, datasets, and evaluation metrics in improving breast cancer detection. Method: A systematic search using the PRISMA guideline was conducted. Four electronic databases (Science Direct, IEEE Explore, SpringerLink, and Scopus) and Google Scholar were searched using specific search strings for online articles published between 2020 and 2024. After applying specified inclusion and exclusion criteria, 91 articles were selected for data extraction, synthesis, and quality assessment. Results: This study reveals that generative AI models are used in breast cancer diagnosis for data augmentation, classification, and segmentation. For data augmentation, GAN has proven to be of highest effectiveness, while transformers have the highest effectiveness in terms of classification and segmentation. This review highlights the growing adoption of various publicly and privately available datasets, which have played a crucial role in training and validating these models. The findings showed the importance of selecting appropriate datasets and metrics to enhance the effectiveness of generative AI models in breast cancer diagnosis. A notable gap identified is the underrepresentation of African populations in the datasets used. Furthermore, the limited applicability of these models in real-world clinical settings is attributed to the lack of explainability. Conclusions: This review provides valuable insights into current practices, identifies existing gaps, and highlights areas for future research, aiming to improve the reliability and applicability of AI-based diagnosis in clinical settings.

articles.title: CRISPR/Cas-Based Molecular Diagnostics for Intestinal Parasites: From Proof-of-Concept to Point-of-Care Testing.
articles.abstract: Intestinal parasitic infections remain a significant global public health concern, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where timely and accurate diagnosis is essential for effective disease management and control. Although conventional diagnostic methods, including microscopy, antigen detection, and polymerase chain reaction (PCR), are widely used, each possesses inherent limitations related to sensitivity, turnaround time, laboratory infrastructure, or point-of-care applicability. Recent advances in clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeat (CRISPR)/CRISPR-associated (Cas) systems have led to the development of highly sensitive and rapid molecular diagnostic platforms suitable for decentralized testing. This review summarizes current applications of CRISPR/Cas-based diagnostics for intestinal and foodborne parasitic infections, with particular emphasis on assays developed for Giardia duodenalis, Cryptosporidium parvum, Clonorchis sinensis, Fasciola hepatica, and Schistosoma spp. Published studies have predominantly employed Cas12a, with additional applications of Cas12b and Cas13a and, more recently, a type I-A Cascade-Cas3 system, generally coupled with isothermal amplification methods such as recombinase polymerase amplification (RPA) or recombinase-aided amplification (RAA), enabling highly sensitive detection within 60-90 min using fluorescence or lateral-flow strip readouts. The available evidence indicates high analytical sensitivity and specificity, with several assays demonstrating substantial agreement with conventional molecular methods and potential for point-of-care development. However, current CRISPR-based assays remain limited by dependence on nucleic acid extraction, relatively small clinical validation cohorts, lack of standardized protocols, and the persistence of false-negative results associated with low parasite burdens and pre-analytical variables. Emerging strategies, including simplified or extraction-free sample preparation, one-pot sample-to-answer platforms, and detection of parasite-derived cell-free DNA, may further enhance the clinical utility of CRISPR diagnostics. Overall, CRISPR/Cas-based technologies represent a promising next-generation approach for intestinal parasite diagnosis, although large-scale clinical validation and workflow optimization are still required before widespread implementation in routine clinical and field settings.

articles.title: Continuous Glucose Monitoring for Metabolic Phenotyping and Precision Nutrition: Current Evidence, Clinical Applications and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) has evolved beyond conventional diabetes management into an enabling technology for metabolic phenotyping and precision nutrition by providing continuous, real-world assessment of individual glycemic responses to dietary and lifestyle exposures. This narrative review examines the principles and clinical utility of CGM and its emerging applications in metabolic monitoring and personalized nutrition, with particular emphasis on postprandial glycemic variability, computational prediction, dietary feedback, and behavioral interventions. A literature search was conducted in Web of Science, PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar using predefined combinations of terms related to CGM, precision and personalized nutrition, diet, postprandial glycemic responses, lifestyle, glycemic variability, artificial intelligence, machine learning, and computational nutrition, including English-language literature available up to June 2026. Current evidence demonstrates substantial interindividual variability in postprandial glycemic responses and supports the potential integration of CGM with dietary, clinical, anthropometric, behavioral, and microbiome-derived data to characterize individual metabolic responses and inform individualized prediction and nutritional guidance. However, the reproducibility and generalizability of CGM-derived metabolic phenotypes and predictive models remain incompletely established. CGM-supported nutritional and behavioral interventions have demonstrated improvements in glycemic and selected cardiometabolic outcomes, particularly in individuals with type 2 diabetes, whereas evidence of clinical benefit in populations without diabetes remains substantially more limited. Sustained engagement and psychological, technical, and accessibility-related limitations also remain important considerations. Emerging multi-analyte sensing technologies may further broaden continuous metabolic assessment and support more comprehensive, data-driven precision-nutrition strategies.

articles.title: Hidden Signals in Serum Protein Electrophoresis: Artificial Intelligence from Laboratory Pattern Recognition to Clinical Validation.
articles.abstract: Serum protein electrophoresis (SPE) remains a central laboratory method for the detection and characterization of monoclonal gammopathies and other dysproteinemic patterns. Despite substantial analytical automation, interpretation still relies largely on graphical representation and expert visual assessment, making low-amplitude or borderline abnormalities particularly challenging. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine-learning (ML) and deep-learning (DL) approaches, has increasingly been applied to SPE, with high performance reported for automated recognition of established abnormalities, particularly M-proteins, i.e., monoclonal immunoglobulins or immunoglobulin fragments produced by clonal plasma cells. However, most models have been developed against predefined diagnostic targets and evaluated using expert interpretation, immunofixation, or immunotyping as reference standards. Improved recognition of known abnormalities should therefore not be equated with discovery of additional clinically meaningful information. Modern electrophoretic platforms generate machine-readable numerical signals that may preserve features not explicitly considered during routine graphical interpretation. This creates the possibility of extending AI-assisted SPE from conventional pattern recognition toward detection of low-amplitude, distributed, or sub-visual signal characteristics. Yet current literature has focused predominantly on algorithmic performance, while the validation pathway required to determine whether additional AI-detected features are biologically meaningful and clinically actionable remains insufficiently defined. Evidence is strongest for automated M-protein recognition, including low-amplitude abnormalities, whereas non-canonical systemic patterns, longitudinal signal analysis, and AI-assisted decomposition of therapeutic monoclonal antibody interference remain exploratory. This critical review addresses this translational gap by evaluating AI applications according to the nature of detected information, strength of supporting evidence, and proximity to clinical implementation. We propose a translational framework addressing four complementary domains: analytical validity, biological validity, clinical validity, and clinical utility. The evidence required in each domain depends on the intended claim and clinical use.

articles.title: Diagnostic Assessment of Tamoxifen-Associated Endometrial Pathology: A Narrative Review of Biomarkers, Risk Models, and Translational Gaps.
articles.abstract: In tamoxifen-related endometrial alterations, a challenge arises due to the similarity between clinically significant diseases and both benign proliferation and benign polyps. This narrative review examines the clinical assessment, imaging, tissue sampling, biomarkers, and prediction models for women taking tamoxifen. We searched PubMed/MEDLINE and selected articles from reference lists up to August 2026, focusing on human studies reporting diagnostic performance, biomarkers, sampling limitations, or clinical prediction. Evidence was divided into three groups: tamoxifen-specific clinical studies, external studies of endometrial cancer, and mechanistic investigations; however, the heterogeneous populations and endpoints prevented pooled accuracy estimates. Although thickening of the endometrium is associated with an increased risk of abnormal bleeding, the finding when there is no abnormal bleeding is not significant enough to warrant routine surveillance of asymptomatic users. Representative histopathology remains the key, especially if hysteroscopy is used for sampling, particularly if the area is focal or if a diagnosis is not reached. These tissue markers primarily reflect the biology of exposure and show promise in methylation, cytology, serum-marker, and prediction studies, mostly in populations that are not tamoxifen-validated. Thus, reported discrimination does not provide sufficient reassurance to exclude atypical hyperplasia or carcinoma in tamoxifen users. The priorities are prospective validation in well-defined symptomatic patient groups, independent validation of locked assays or models against clinical baseline, and a focus on missed significant disease, avoided procedures, and patient outcomes. The current evidence favors a cautious diagnostic evaluation and does not define a biomarker-based screening or surveillance approach for women taking tamoxifen.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence Applications in Laser-Assisted Refractive Surgery-A Comprehensive Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Artificial Intelligence (AI) technology-in the form of Machine Learning (ML) models and other models specialized in image recognition and processing, such as Convolutional Neural Networks Visual Transformers (CNN-ViTs)-is increasingly being used in ophthalmology. This review summarizes the main AI applications for laser-assisted refractive surgery. Methods: A wide-ranging literature search on the PubMed and ISI Thompson Web of Science databases was conducted. Results: AI is an all-encompassing technological concept that refers to either specific applications of ML/CNN models, such as in keratoconus screening or diagnosis, or agentic/multimodal AI applications that process different data types using a variety of AI models. The most clinically established applications found were corneal ectasia and keratoconus screening, in which AI models can reliably exceed 95% diagnostic accuracy, specificity, and sensitivity; nomogram-derived laser ablation programming; optimization of ray-tracing calculations for ray-traced ablation profiles; patient screening and selection for refractive surgery; visual and refractive result prediction; assessment of postoperative corneal ectasia risk; detection of intraoperative complications; research on the laser coupling effect; and other applications such as monitoring eye rubbing behavior in corneal ectasia suspects. Thus, singular, specific applications of AI models have made the largest clinical contributions. These results must be interpreted with a comparison of internal versus external validation, calibration, and generalizability. Overall the technology is highly promising. Agentic/multimodal AI frameworks are currently being discussed, with pilot studies published and applicability proposed in the context of large, high-patient-volume clinical practices. The technological advent of SHAP force plot graphs and saliency maps has improved understanding of the factors that contribute mechanistically to AI model reasoning, leading to more informed clinical decisions or research applicability, such as in finding parameters or factors linked to postoperative ectasia. Conclusions: AI is already established in laser-assisted refractive surgery in the form of models specialized in data-intensive analysis. At present, the best-performing novel AI models originate from the domain of large or multi-hospital settings due to requirements for multiple latest-generation diagnostic devices, high-volume patient data, computing expertise, and resources. Future directions could include clinical standardization and trickle-down dissemination of the technology. Agentic/multimodal AI has the potential to benefit large clinical/patient settings or offer access to expert knowledge in smaller practice settings. Agentic/multimodal AI implementation is offset by challenges in complexity, the technological limitations of LLMs ("hallucinations"), and ethical and legislative factors.

articles.title: Plasma and Serum Metagenomic Sequencing of Microbial Cell-Free Nucleic Acids for Suspected Central Nervous System Infection: A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Untargeted metagenomic sequencing of microbial cell-free DNA or RNA in plasma or serum offers pathogen detection without lumbar puncture or biopsy, but its value in suspected central nervous system (CNS) infection is uncertain. We reviewed diagnostic yield, agreement with CNS-site testing, clinical impact, and failure modes. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE was searched with seven documented strings (inception to 2 September 2026), supplemented by citation and web searching. Eligible reports were primary human studies of untargeted plasma or serum metagenomic sequencing with a separable result in patients with suspected or confirmed infectious CNS syndromes. Selection, extraction, and design-specific risk-of-bias appraisal followed PRISMA 2020 and were performed independently by two authors with disagreements resolved by discussion; the search was restricted to PubMed/MEDLINE and no protocol was registered. Synthesis was narrative because designs and reference standards were incompatible. Results: Of 190 reports assessed, 69 studies were included (18 denominator-based cohorts, 8 small series, 43 case reports; 51 from the United States). Positive CNS-specific clinical impact in commercial assay cohorts ranged from 0 of 24 adult to 5 of 24 pediatric meningoencephalitis tests. Among 51 case-level reports, the plasma or serum result was concordant with CNS-site testing in 28, positive when CNS-site testing was negative in 5, unconfirmed in 12, and negative or missed the pathogen in 6. All five plasma-only detections came from single case reports, which contributed to no yield or agreement denominator; excluding the four abstract-level case reports moved no proportion by more than 1.3 percentage points. RNA viruses, low-burden focal mould disease, and chromosomally integrated HHV-6 were recurrent sources of false-negative or misleading results. Conclusions: Plasma or serum metagenomic sequencing is a useful adjunct in selected difficult CNS infections, particularly disseminated, fungal, amoebic, or fastidious bacterial disease, but it does not replace CNS-site diagnostics.

articles.title: Biomarkers in Acute Mesenteric Ischemia: A Systematic Review of Diagnostic Performance and Injury-Related Signals.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: We examined nine biomarkers for acute mesenteric ischemia (AMI) detection, necrosis and postoperative prediction. Methods: PubMed/MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library and indexed citation links were searched on 10 October 2026 without a lower publication-year limit. PubMed and citation searches used an October 2026 publication cutoff. English- and Russian-language clinical reports with at least 10 participants were eligible. Narrative synthesis used QUADAS-2 and diagnostic GRADE. Results: Twenty-nine primary reports were included, with reported cohorts of 18-1479 participants. Cohort overlap and varying tested denominators precluded an unduplicated participant total. Among 28 diagnostic reports, 22 had high index-test risk and 25 had high flow/timing risk. Certainty was very low for eight markers. I-FABP, α-GST and citrulline findings depended on population, assay and timing. D-dimer, lactate, procalcitonin and ischemia-modified albumin lacked intestinal specificity. Urinary I-FABP estimates were imprecise. SM22 supplied association data without diagnostic-performance estimates. Conclusions: No evaluated marker supports reliable stand-alone exclusion of AMI or determination of bowel viability. Complementary panels require prospective validation. The injury diagrams are unvalidated research models.

articles.title: Heart Failure Beyond the Heart: Digestive-System Involvement and Its Diagnostic and Prognostic Implications-A Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Heart failure (HF) is a systemic syndrome in which congestion, hypoperfusion, inflammation and neurohormonal activation may affect the liver, splanchnic circulation, intestinal barrier, pancreas, biliary system and nutritional state. This systematic review synthesised clinical evidence on digestive-system involvement in adults with established HF and examined its diagnostic and prognostic implications within a cautious cardio-gastrointestinal syndrome (CGIS) framework. Methods: The structured synthesis was based on an audited historical review register. The original project record reported 815 records before deduplication, although source-specific yields and the citation-level deduplication trail could not be reconstructed from the preserved files. A reproducibility-validation rerun was executed on 8 August 2026 in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus and Web of Science Core Collection, targeting literature through 1 July 2026; exact day-level cutoff reproducibility differed by database. The rerun recovered all ten benchmark reference-set reports but was not used to redefine the historical corpus and does not establish search exhaustiveness. The final 29-report register was re-audited for eligibility, design, analysed sample, principal findings and cohort overlap. Owing to substantial heterogeneity, findings were synthesised narratively. Results: 29 eligible reports represented approximately 26 cohort families. Hepatic and splanchnic involvement was the most mature evidence cluster, followed by intestinal congestion/barrier dysfunction. Pancreatic, biliary, microbiota and nutritional findings were less independently replicated. Liver biochemistry, composite hepatic scores and venous Doppler phenotypes showed marker-specific prognostic associations. Intestinal oedema was associated with impaired oral diuretic response. Direct pancreatic exocrine-insufficiency evidence was limited to faecal-elastase assessment. Conclusions: Digestive involvement in HF is clinically coherent but unevenly evidenced. CGIS is best regarded as a hypothesis-generating framework rather than a validated diagnostic entity, and prospective standardised studies are required before organ-specific biomarkers or imaging thresholds enter routine algorithms.

articles.title: Diagnostic Accuracy and Renal Safety of Carbon Dioxide Angiography in Lower Limb Angiography: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Iodinated contrast media (ICM) used in lower limb angiography carry risks of contrast-induced nephropathy (CIN) and allergic reactions, particularly in patients with peripheral arterial disease (PAD) and renal dysfunction. Carbon dioxide (CO2) angiography offers a potential non-nephrotoxic alternative. The purpose of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy and renal safety of CO2 angiography compared with ICM in patients undergoing lower limb angiography for PAD. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was performed from inception to 4 September 2025. Studies comparing CO2 angiography with ICM in adult PAD patients were included. Risk of bias was assessed with QUADAS-2 for diagnostic accuracy studies and RoB 2 for randomised trials, and the methodological quality of comparative observational studies with the Newcastle-Ottawa Scale. Pooled sensitivity, specificity, adverse events, CIN, contrast volume, serum creatinine, and estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) were analysed using random-effects models. Results: Nine studies (527 patients) were included. In three studies (111 patients) with extractable diagnostic accuracy data, CO2 angiography showed pooled sensitivity of 0.89 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.78-0.95) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI: 0.85-0.99). Adverse events did not differ significantly between groups (four studies; risk ratio [RR] 0.63, 95% CI: 0.15-2.71), but discomfort during CO2 injection was common. CIN risk was lower with CO2 (two studies; RR 0.31, 95% CI: 0.14-0.73; p = 0.007), and contrast volume was reduced by a mean of 80.71 mL (two studies; p < 0.00001). Pooled serum creatinine and eGFR estimates showed extreme heterogeneity (I2 = 98-99%), with the two contributing studies reporting effects in opposite directions. Conclusions: In a small number of comparative studies, CO2 angiography showed pooled sensitivity and specificity compatible with clinically useful diagnostic performance, although these exploratory estimates derive from three studies with unblinded reference standards. The lower risk of CIN with CO2, observed in two studies, is hypothesis-generating, and CO2 has adverse effects of its own, principally discomfort during injection. These findings should be confirmed in larger prospective trials before CO2 can be regarded as an established alternative for patients at risk of CIN or iodine allergy.

articles.title: Combined Approach with Ultrasound and Pressure-Volume Loops to Manage Mechanical Ventilation in Acute Hypoxemic Respiratory Failure.
articles.abstract: Acute hypoxemic respiratory failure (AHRF), particularly acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), is characterized by marked heterogeneity in lung morphology and mechanics, requiring individualized mechanical ventilation strategies that balance adequate gas exchange with the prevention of ventilator-induced lung injury (VILI). Lung ultrasound (LUS) has become a cornerstone of critical care imaging, allowing differential diagnosis, quantitative assessment of lung aeration, phenotyping of ARDS morphology, and monitoring of disease evolution and complications. However, imaging alone does not provide direct guidance for optimizing ventilator settings. Some modern ventilators enable the rapid bedside acquisition of tidal pressure-volume (PV) loops, allowing tidal hysteresis to be measured and thereby providing complementary physiological information by identifying cyclic opening and closing of lung units and signs of overdistension. Emerging evidence supports the use of tidal hysteresis thresholds to identify insufficient positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) associated with tidal recruitment/derecruitment and to guide individualized PEEP titration during decremental PEEP trials. This review discusses the rationale and practical implementation of an integrated approach combining critical care ultrasound and PV loops throughout the management of mechanically ventilated patients with AHRF. We describe how ultrasound can support diagnosis, phenotyping, monitoring of lung aeration, and detection of ventilation-related complications, while PV loops provide a practical physiological framework for optimizing ventilator settings. This approach may provide a comprehensive, non-invasive, and repeatable bedside assessment of lung morphology, aeration, and respiratory mechanics, potentially facilitating personalized mechanical ventilation strategies aimed at reducing the risk of VILI and optimizing patient management.

articles.title: AI-Driven Hyperspectral Imaging in Clinical Medicine: A Critical Appraisal of Translational Readiness.
articles.abstract: The instruments used for intraoperative guidance have not improved over the years. Traditional margin evaluations fail in 10-20% of cancer surgeries, and histopathology confirmation can take 48-72 h. A promising alternative is hyperspectral imaging (HSI), which allows for real-time, label-free, non-contact, and detailed biochemical characterization of tissues. This review synthesizes 130 studies from 2015 to 2026, identified through a systematic search across multiple databases following PRISMA-ScR guidelines. The studies cover various clinical areas, including surgical oncology (53%), neurosurgery (10.8%), perfusion assessment (6.2%), gastroenterology (5.4%), dermatology (4.6%), and emerging domains (20%). Each clinical area is evaluated using a four-part Translational Readiness Appraisal framework. This framework shifts the focus from technical proficiency to deployment evidence by examining hardware compatibility with operating rooms, real-time workflow integration, cross-site validation, and regulatory readiness. Since 2015, the combination of clinically approved HSI hardware and artificial intelligence has led to a tenfold increase in publications. However, a significant gap remains: none of the reviewed studies meet the evidence criteria necessary for regulatory approval. Of the studies, 48.5% show strong single-site validation, but 50.8% remain in the proof-of-concept stage. The heavy reliance on intra-patient validation tends to inflate performance estimates, leaving issues like calibration across devices and regulatory pathways largely unaddressed. HSI has demonstrated technical maturity in several areas, particularly in head and neck margin assessment and brain tumor delineation. The primary reason for the lack of clinical adoption is not imaging performance but rather the absence of multicenter validation and a formal regulatory evidence framework.

articles.title: Cell-Free DNA-Based Blood Tests for Colorectal Cancer Screening: Current Advances, Challenges, and Future Perspectives.
articles.abstract: Background: Colorectal cancer (CRC) is a major cause of rising global rates of cancer-related morbidity and mortality. CRC rates are particularly increasing among younger populations; however, the implementation of effective CRC screening programs remains limited. Colonoscopy, the gold standard CRC screening technique, is restricted by complex procedures, invasive methods, and low patient adherence. Therefore, non-invasive screening through circulating cell-free DNA (cfDNA)-based blood tests is emerging as an effective alternative. Methods: This narrative review summarizes recent advances in cfDNA-based blood tests for colorectal cancer screening and early detection. Relevant English-language publications from 2021 to 2025 were searched on PubMed, ScienceDirect, and Google Scholar databases, supplemented by examination of reference lists. The study evaluated various diagnostic performance measures [sensitivity, specificity, and AUC (area under the curve)] and compared cfDNA-based approaches with previously established screening methods. Results: CRC detection and diagnostic efficacies of cfDNA-based technologies (mutation analysis, fragmentomics, integrated multi-omics approaches, and methylation profiling) have been reported in several recent studies. Fragmentomics and integrated multi-omics strategies have reported high diagnostic accuracy in a small number of heterogeneous, non-pooled studies. During a large-scale ECLIPSE study, involving an average-risk screening population, the Shield blood-based assay demonstrated 83.1% sensitivity for CRC, whereas the sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions was only 13.2%. However, lack of assay standardization, low sensitivity for advanced precancerous lesions, methodological heterogeneity, and the need for prospective validation before routine clinical implementation remain major limitations. Conclusions: cfDNA-based non-invasive screening tools offer promising colorectal cancer detection accuracy. However, prospective validation, standardization, and optimization of analytical workflows are mandatory for the widespread clinical implementation of these techniques.

articles.title: Pyonephrosis-An Updated Morphological Glimpse into the Contemporary Management of an Immemorial Pathology: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Pyonephrosis-pus within an obstructed, infected renal collecting system, with suppurative parenchymal destruction-is a urological emergency and a potentially reversible cause of acute kidney injury (AKI); a contribution to chronic kidney disease (CKD) is biologically plausible but has not been demonstrated in pyonephrosis-specific longitudinal studies. This narrative review, reported with reference to the SANRA criteria and based on structured searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, synthesizes the epidemiology, pathophysiology, microbiology, morphological diagnosis, and contemporary management of pyonephrosis, distinguishing evidence generated in confirmed pyonephrosis from that in infected hydronephrosis, obstructive pyelonephritis, and stone-associated sepsis. Sonographic, computed tomographic, and magnetic resonance features are illustrated with original schematics and a case of perforated calculous pyonephrosis; reported Hounsfield-unit thresholds and apparent diffusion coefficients derive from small, single-center cohorts and are protocol- and population-dependent rather than universal cut-offs. Urgent decompression is strongly recommended by guidelines, but the supporting data are observational, so associations between drainage, its timing, and mortality remain vulnerable to confounding. Randomized comparisons of percutaneous nephrostomy and retrograde stenting are few, small, and inconsistent, and establish neither superiority nor equivalence in infected systems. We rate the certainty of each principal conclusion and identify research priorities.

articles.title: Genetic Predictors of Curve Progression and Brace Treatment Response in Adolescent Idiopathic Scoliosis: Toward Personalized Management.
articles.abstract: Adolescent idiopathic scoliosis (AIS) is characterized by substantial variability in curve progression and response to conservative treatment, making accurate prognostic assessment a major clinical challenge. Although established clinical and radiographic factors contribute to risk stratification, they do not fully explain individual differences in disease evolution or brace treatment outcome. This review critically examines current evidence on genetic determinants of curve progression and brace treatment response in AIS, with particular emphasis on their potential contribution to individualized risk prediction. Candidate-gene studies have reported associations involving hormonal, metabolic, developmental, and skeletal pathways, while studies of brace response have identified potential predictive associations involving ERα, TPH1, VDR, VDBP, and BNC2. Multigene approaches, including ScoliScore, have further explored the potential of polygenic information for prognostic assessment. However, reported genetic effects are generally modest, replication across populations remains limited, and substantial heterogeneity exists in study design, outcome definitions, and characterization of brace treatment. Importantly, current evidence remains insufficient to demonstrate clinically meaningful predictive value of genetic information beyond established clinical factors. Future research should prioritize large prospective multicenter cohorts, standardized definitions of progression and treatment outcome, objective assessment of brace adherence and correction, progression-specific polygenic approaches, and external validation across diverse populations. Ultimately, integrating genetic information with clinical, radiographic, developmental, biomechanical, and treatment-related variables may provide a more comprehensive framework for individualized prediction and precision management of AIS.

articles.title: Artificial Intelligence-Enhanced Cardiac Magnetic Resonance in Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy: Diagnosis, Phenotypic Characterization, and Risk Prediction.
articles.abstract: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is a genetically and phenotypically heterogeneous myocardial disease associated with a broad spectrum of clinical outcomes, including heart failure, atrial fibrillation, ventricular arrhythmias, and sudden cardiac death. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) plays a central role in the comprehensive assessment of HCM by enabling integrated evaluation of myocardial morphology, ventricular and atrial function, tissue characterization, myocardial deformation, and longitudinal disease progression within a single comprehensive imaging modality. However, conventional CMR interpretation remains limited by manual post-processing, interobserver variability, sequence-dependent measurements, and reliance on a relatively restricted set of predefined imaging parameters. These limitations may hinder the full exploitation of the rich multidimensional information contained in CMR datasets. Artificial intelligence (AI) approaches, particularly machine learning and deep learning, together with radiomics-based quantitative image analysis, provide new opportunities to extend the diagnostic and prognostic value of CMR to extract high-dimensional and quantitative information from cine imaging, late gadolinium enhancement, parametric mapping, and feature-tracking-based deformation analysis. Emerging evidence suggests that AI-enhanced CMR may facilitate automated image analysis, improve diagnostic classification, support differentiation of HCM from phenocopies, enable tissue- and deformation-based phenotypic characterization, and enhance individualized risk prediction. Although several studies have included independent or external testing, many remain retrospective, rely on selected populations or internal validation, and lack prospective assessment of clinical utility. High discrimination performance should not be interpreted as established clinical utility, because calibration, decision-curve analysis, clinically relevant thresholds, and prospective clinical impact remain insufficiently evaluated. In addition, interpretability and clinical generalizability remain important challenges for translation into routine practice. This review summarizes the current role of CMR in HCM and discusses emerging applications, methodological challenges, and future directions of AI-enhanced CMR for diagnosis, phenotypic characterization, and risk stratification.

articles.title: Radiomics-Based Outcome Prediction in Transarterial Radioembolization (TARE) of Hepatic Malignancies: A Systematic Review and Quality Appraisal.
articles.abstract: Background: Transarterial radioembolization (TARE) with Yttrium-90 (90Y) microspheres is an established locoregional treatment for primary and secondary hepatic malignancies. Treatment response is heterogeneous, and accurate pre-procedural prediction of outcome remains a clinical challenge. Radiomics, defined as the high-throughput extraction of quantitative imaging features, may capture subvisual tumour heterogeneity that might be predictive of response, therefore enabling individualised patient selection and treatment planning. Objectives: To systematically review the current evidence on radiomics-based models derived from pre- and post-procedural imaging for predicting treatment response and survival outcomes in patients with primary and secondary hepatic lesions that were treated with TARE, and to evaluate the methodological quality of included studies. Methods: A systematic literature search was conducted across PubMed, Embase, Scopus, and Web of Science. Studies reporting radiomics, texture analysis, dosiomics, or machine learning applied to imaging in patients with hepatic lesions treated with TARE, with at least one reported performance metric, were included. Methodological quality was assessed using the Radiomics Quality Score (RQS) and risk of bias and applicability using the Prediction model Risk Of Bias ASsessment Tool (PROBAST). Due to substantial heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was performed. Results: Twenty-one studies encompassing 1734 patients were included (up to 73 patients may be counted twice because two cohorts overlap). Studies evaluated patients with hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC; n = 12), intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (iCC; n = 2), colorectal cancer liver metastases (CLMs; n = 3), and mixed tumour cohorts (n = 4). Imaging modalities included MRI (n = 9), CT (n = 5), 18F-FDG PET or PET/CT (n = 3), 90Y PET or SPECT (n = 2), cone-beam CT (n = 1), and CT perfusion (n = 1). All studies were retrospective, including two post hoc analyses of randomised trial cohorts, and none used external validation. Eighteen studies reported an area under the curve (AUC). The highest reported AUC ranged from 0.71 to 0.90 in eight studies with no validation, from 0.73 to 1.00 in six studies using internal cross-validation, and from 0.80 to 0.90 in four studies using an internal hold-out set. The median RQS was 2 (interquartile range 1 to 5; maximum 36), and all 21 studies had a high overall risk of bias on PROBAST. Conclusions: Radiomic models for predicting TARE outcomes show moderate to high apparent discrimination, but the evidence comes from small retrospective cohorts, is at high risk of bias, and has not been externally validated. Adding clinical variables to radiomic features produced only small gains. Prospective, multi-centre studies with standardised segmentation, harmonised radiomics pipelines, and robust external validation are needed before routine clinical adoption.

articles.title: Diagnostic Contribution of Histopathology in Medicolegal Autopsy: A Denominator-Specific Systematic Review.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Published estimates of histopathological examination (HPE) contribution in medicolegal autopsy use different denominators and outcome definitions. We examined what these estimates measure and their implications for practice. Methods: PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Scopus were searched from inception to 31 May 2026 (PROSPERO CRD420261401909). Eligible studies reported denominator-specific HPE contribution. Cause of death (COD) provision and change were distinguished from manner change, confirmation, refinement, and targeted forensic interpretation. JBI checklists supported item-level appraisal. Findings were synthesized narratively without pooling. Results: Twenty-one studies were included from 2287 identified records. Strict COD change was reported in 0/100 uncomplicated hanging suicides and 1/189 gross-clear medicolegal autopsies. A broad systematic-histology cohort reported histology-only COD provision in 36/428 cases. In separate unresolved-COD populations, studies reported COD provision in 49/203 and 40/71 cases. These results address different diagnostic questions and do not establish a relationship between uncertainty and yield. Selected denominators, composite outcomes, and incomplete separation from other investigations limited interpretation. Confirmation, injury assessment, and organ-specific findings represented additional functions. Conclusions: There is no single transferable HPE yield: the pre-HPE diagnosis, denominator, outcome definition, and contribution of other investigations must accompany each estimate. The review supports clearer reporting and interpretation of HPE contribution; low rates of COD change do not establish when histology can safely be omitted.

articles.title: Role of Ultrasonography in the Diagnosis of Splenic Diseases.
articles.abstract: The spleen, which serves as an important indicator of disease activity in various disorders, is routinely examined during abdominal ultrasonography. Although splenic ultrasonography has received relatively little attention compared with that focused on the liver and pancreas, recent advances in ultrasound technology have markedly improved its diagnostic capability. This mini-review re-evaluates the current role of ultrasonography in splenic imaging, focusing on recent technological developments and their clinical applications. Wide-scanning (WS) technology expands the field of view from approximately 70° to 140°, enabling visualization of the entire spleen within a single image. This may facilitate more reliable assessment of splenic size and peripheral lesions and can be combined with Doppler ultrasonography and contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS). Microvascular flow imaging (MVFI) techniques, including Superb Microvascular Imaging and B-flow imaging, provide high-frame-rate imaging with excellent sensitivity for slow blood flow, allowing more detailed assessment of the intralesional vascularity and potentially aiding the evaluation of splenic tumors and infarctions. Splenic elastography offers a non-invasive assessment of portal hypertension and, when interpreted together with liver stiffness, may provide additional diagnostic information in non-cirrhotic portal hypertension. CEUS provides real-time assessment of splenic perfusion and lesion enhancement and may aid the characterization of focal lesions and the evaluation of splenic infarction. However, spleen-specific evidence remains limited, with much of the available literature consisting of small observational studies, case series, and case reports. Based on the available literature and our clinical experience, we also propose a practical multiparametric approach to splenic ultrasonography; however, this approach should be regarded as a clinically oriented framework rather than a prospectively validated diagnostic algorithm.

articles.title: Imaging and Management of Scoliosis-Related Low Back Pain in Adolescents and Adults.
articles.abstract: Background/Objectives: Low back pain (LBP) is a clinically relevant symptom in adolescents and adults with scoliosis, but its relationship with curve magnitude is inconsistent, and curve measurement alone therefore cannot explain symptom burden or direct pain management. This narrative review examines imaging findings and clinically plausible mechanisms of scoliosis-related LBP, considered separately for adolescent idiopathic scoliosis, adult idiopathic scoliosis, adult degenerative scoliosis and adult spinal deformity, and their implications for management. Methods: This narrative review was conducted and reported with reference to the SANRA quality domains. PubMed and the Cochrane Library were searched between June and July 2026, with database-specific search strings, search dates and record yields reported in full. Study selection was performed by the first author and reviewed by the co-authors, without independent duplicate screening or formal risk-of-bias assessment. Results: Curve magnitude is not a consistent independent predictor of pain burden, and pain distribution does not reliably follow curve laterality in adult degenerative scoliosis. We propose an author-derived and prospectively unvalidated seven-component framework comprising five candidate pain generators-facet-mediated, vertebrogenic/endplate, foraminal or lateral recess compression, sagittal malalignment with paraspinal overload, and sacroiliac overload-together with biopsychosocial pain modifiers and associated neural-axis abnormalities. Imaging may identify clinically plausible contributors but cannot establish pain causation in isolation; clinical concordance and, for selected interventions, supportive diagnostic procedures remain essential. Standing full-spine radiography, or low-dose biplanar acquisition where serial monitoring is required in adolescents, provides structural and alignment assessment, whereas MRI should be tailored to the clinical scenario and differs in purpose between adolescents and adults. Evidence supporting mechanism-directed interventions derives largely from non-scoliotic chronic LBP cohorts and is identified as such throughout. Conclusions: Imaging in scoliosis-related LBP should identify clinically concordant candidate pain sources rather than merely quantify deformity. Structural abnormalities are not synonymous with pain generators, and treatment selection should integrate imaging with clinical assessment and, when appropriate, supportive diagnostic procedures. The proposed framework and management pathway are author-derived and require prospective validation.

articles.title: Advances in Diagnostic Testing for Eosinophilic Esophagitis: Current Approaches, Limitations, and Emerging Technologies.
articles.abstract: Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic disease of the esophagus caused by an abnormal type 2 (Th2) immune response. It is a leading cause of dysphagia in both pediatric and adult populations. Endoscopy with biopsy remains the standard approach for diagnosis, but its invasive nature and need for repeated procedures have prompted investigation of alternative and complementary approaches. A narrative review was conducted to synthesize evidence on established and emerging modalities for EoE diagnosis and disease assessment, including minimally invasive sampling techniques, functional and structural assessment, mucosal impedance, molecular diagnostics, tissue-based assessment, and artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted approaches. Minimally invasive approaches may facilitate diagnosis or longitudinal monitoring, while complementary modalities provide assessment of structural, functional, histologic, and molecular features of disease. In retrospective image datasets, AI models have demonstrated high performance for automated eosinophil quantification and detection f endoscopic features, although none has been prospectively validated in routine clinical practice. Despite these advances, widespread adoption remains limited by cost, accessibility, and variability in validation across diverse populations. Further prospective and external validation is needed to establish the role of these modalities in mainstream practice.

articles.title: From Measured Accuracy to Patient Outcome: Navigation in Total Hip Arthroplasty and Molecular Diagnosis of Periprosthetic Joint Infection: A Narrative Review.
articles.abstract: Background: Total hip arthroplasty (THA) and the diagnosis of periprosthetic joint infection (PJI) have each acquired a technology that measures with high precision: intraoperative navigation, which reports component position to within a few degrees, and molecular methods, which identify the infecting organism and the host response at genomic resolution. Objective: To establish whether the measured accuracy has been shown to reach the patient as a clinical outcome. Methods: This is a narrative review, reported according to SANRA. MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science databases were searched from inception to 31 August 2026. English-language studies in humans were eligible if they reported positional or diagnostic accuracy, a patient-level clinical or economic outcome after THA or after treatment of PJI or osteomyelitis, or a factor modifying the relation between the two. Animal, in vitro, and cadaveric studies, conference abstracts, and reports without extractable data were excluded. Forty studies were included. No pooled estimate was calculated, and no new statistical analysis was performed. Results: Navigation reduced positional outliers consistently, but in two matched claims-based cohorts of patients with morbid obesity (4499 and 5835 patients), it was not associated with lower rates of PJI, dislocation, periprosthetic fracture, mechanical loosening, or revision within two years. Candidate immunogenetic variants in osteomyelitis have never been tested against a treatment decision. Metagenomic sequencing was no more accurate than culture (sensitivity 63.2% versus 68.4%; specificity 80.0% versus 95.0%) except after antibiotic exposure. Reported infection rates and test accuracy both change with the case definition applied. Conclusions: In both settings, the limiting factor is the design of the studies linking measurement to outcome rather than the precision of the measurement.

articles.title: The Salivary Healing Signature: From Disease Detection to Prediction and Monitoring of Periodontal and Peri-Implant Tissue Healing.
articles.abstract: Periodontal and peri-implant diseases cause progressive tissue destruction that may lead to tooth and implant loss. Conventional clinical and radiographic assessments document accumulated tissue damage but provide limited information on current biological activity or healing. This narrative review synthesizes the literature published between 2015 and 2025, identified through searches of PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, and Web of Science, on salivary biomarkers in periodontal and peri-implant diseases, with emphasis on diagnostic performance, changes after therapy, and clinical translation. Salivary inflammatory mediators and tissue- and bone-remodeling markers-including interleukin (IL)-1β, IL-6, IL-8, IL-17, tumor necrosis factor-α, matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-8, MMP-9, calprotectin, and the RANKL/osteoprotegerin axis-are consistently associated with periodontal and peri-implant disease. Multimarker panels generally outperform single biomarkers, with some studies reporting areas under the curve above 0.90 for periodontitis detection; however, most evidence derives from cross-sectional diagnostic studies, and prospective prognostic data remain limited. We propose the "salivary healing signature" as a conceptual framework-not a validated test-in which serial multimarker measurements could complement clinical assessment for disease detection, risk stratification, and treatment monitoring. Standardized sampling and analytical protocols, control of confounders, defined thresholds, and prospective validation in diverse populations are required before clinical implementation.

articles.title: Vascular Phenotyping Across the CKM Syndrome: Arterial Stiffness and Endothelial Function Testing, Prognostic Value and Clinical Implementation.
articles.abstract: Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) syndrome represents a continuum of metabolic, renal, and cardiovascular abnormalities in which vascular dysfunction may develop before clinically overt cardiovascular disease. Endothelial dysfunction, arterial stiffness, microvascular abnormalities, and structural vascular damage may therefore provide complementary information regarding vascular injury across CKM stages.
